I am sixty-four years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou since I was a boy. My father taught me the wheat-corn rotation, and I have never seen a reason to change it. The grain station always buys both crops, and I know the work with my hands even though I never went to school.

This spring, my winter wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October, as I always do. I have about six mu of good flat land. All six mu will go to wheat, and after I harvest it around early June, I will plant summer corn on the same plots without ploughing again. I do not grow cotton anymore; my back is not what it was, and cotton needs too much bending and pruning. Wheat and corn can be harvested by machine, which is better for a man my age.

For the wheat, I will irrigate three more times before harvest — the winter irrigation is already done, but the spring needs water. I will topdress with urea when the wheat turns green, and spray for insects two or three times. There will be one herbicide and one fungicide as well. I use improved wheat seed that I saved from last year, and I apply compound fertilizer as basal and urea as topdressing.

For the corn, I will buy hybrid seed by the package from the dealer — I usually get Denghai or Nongda varieties. I will not till the soil after wheat; I will drill the corn straight into the stubble. One or two irrigations will be enough for the summer crop, and I will spray for insects twice and apply herbicide once.

I keep my inputs moderate. I know the land, and I do not waste money on things that do not pay back.
